newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan officials may scrap trips over Peru crisis.
newsitem.headline: Japan officials may scrap trips over Peru crisis.

text.p: Japan's prime minister and foreign minister are both considering cancelling foreign trips in January because of the continuing hostage crisis in Lima, Foreign Ministry officials said on Thursday.

And in another sign of Japan's concern over the nine-day-old hostage affair, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto criticised Uruguay's separate deal with Marxist Peruvian guerrillas to win the release of its ambassador, who was among those held hostage at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima.
"The Uruguay government has explained that there was no link between the two (release of the two rebels and the Lima hostage issue)," Hashimoto told reporters.
"I don't know whether this is true or not, but in any case it has made a solution of the case difficult," Hashimoto said. "We must not surrender to terrorism."
More than 100 hostages remain confined in the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima by armed Marxist guerrillas, who stormed the residence on December 17.
The Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas freed the Uruguay ambassador to Peru on Tuesday following the Uruguay government's release from prison of two of their fellow members.
Uruguay denied it had negotiated a swap, but a well-placed Uruguayan government source told Reuters a deal was struck.
Peru recalled its top diplomat in Uruguay on Wednesday in an apparent protest.
On Wednesday, the armed guerrillas released a sick Japanese diplomat. Among the hostages they still hold are top Peruvian politicians, Japanese ambassador Morihisa Aoki and Japanese businessmen.

Chief Cabinet Secretary Seiroku Kajiyama, Japan's top government spokesman, declined to comment on whether there was disagreement between countries on the release of Uruguayan ambassador Tobare Bocalandro Yapeyu.
"I will refrain from commenting immediately on any assumption or on whether there has been disagreement among countries concerned," Kajiyama told a news conference.

In a clear sign that the crisis could drag on into the New Year, Japanese Foreign Ministry officials said Hashimoto may call off a tour of five Southeast Asian countries in January if the crisis is not resolved.
Hashimoto was scheduled to visit Malaysia, Indonesia, Vietnam, Singapore and Brunei between January 7 and 14. All are members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
The ministry officials said they did not know when Hashimoto would announce a formal decision to cancel his trip.
Separately, Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda may also cancel a scheduled trip to Britain and India early next month, the ministry officials said.
Ikeda has already scrubbed a two-day trip to South Korea that was supposed to start on Friday.
Ikeda reaffirmed on Thursday that the Japanese and Peruvian governments had agreed to make efforts to seek a peaceful end to the hostage crisis.

"The Japanese and Peruvian governments are in complete agreement to seek a peaceful end to the situation, without harm to the hostages. We appreciate the Peruvian government's efforts," Ikeda told a parliament session.
"I cannot speak of the possibility of an end to the hostage situation because any such information might work against our efforts to seek such a resolution," Ikeda said.
